tier_reason: The repository README has no numbers, but it cites three peer-reviewed papers (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 2011 and 2024, J. Comput. Phys. 2018) that compare implicit against explicit zero-padded FFTW convolutions; a WebSearch summary of the 2011 paper (arXiv 1008.1366) states the gain as 'by as much as a factor of 2'. Timing code is public (tests/timing.py, tests/timing/timing, hybridconv* tests) but no CPU, compiler or flags are given on any page opened, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'in 2D and 3D implicit zero-padding substantially reduces memory usage and computation time' (no numbers on the repository). Per a WebSearch summary of Bowman and Roberts, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 33:1 (2011) / arXiv 1008.1366 (the paper itself was not opened): increased data locality 'significantly enhanced performance by as much as a factor of 2', and an implicit complex convolution needs one-half the memory of a zero-padded one in 2D and one-quarter in 3D (centered Hermitian: 2/3 in 2D, 4/9 in 3D).
corrections.caveats: No numbers on the repository page; the speedup (up to about 2x over explicit zero-padded convolutions, plus 2-4x less memory in 2D/3D) comes from the peer-reviewed papers, seen here only through a WebSearch summary because arxiv.org, math.ualberta.ca, archive.org and doi.org are blocked in this container. The baseline is explicit zero padding implemented by the same authors on top of FFTW, so this is an algorithmic win for dealiased convolutions, not a faster FFT kernel. Timing scripts are public (tests/timing.py, tests/timing/timing) but no timing data, CPU, compiler or flags are committed. GitHub shows GPL-3.0 and LGPL-3.0 files (LICENSE, LICENSE.LESSER); the README states LGPL v3 or later. The vcpkg port is pinned to a 2019 snapshot.

notes: README and the tests/ and tests/timing/ listings checked; no committed results. Papers unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED for math.ualberta.ca and archive.org); the 'factor of 2' figure comes from a WebSearch summary, so an enricher with paper access should confirm it. Metadata matches: 140 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-08-12 (fix for issue #26).

tier_reason: The README quotes 30x vs gpuNUFFT and 75x vs IRT from a peer-reviewed Magnetic Resonance in Medicine paper (2019, doi 10.1002/mrm.27497), and the repository holds the paper's reproduction scripts (src/RUNME1_tron_degrid_phantom.sh, src/RUNME3_tron_grid_all.sh, MATLAB parts in src/matlab_files.tar.gz) with nvcc flags in src/Makefile. No GPU or CPU model is stated on any page opened, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'TRON is 30x faster than gpuNUFFT (a fast GPU code) and 75x faster than the image reconstruction toolbox (IRT) of Fessler (a ubiquitous CPU-based Matlab code)', with '50% less code than the minimal subset of IRT tested'. The paper abstract, seen only through a WebSearch summary, gives a range: '6-30x faster than the closest competitor, depending on test data set', and over 25x faster than gpuNUFFT; the README's 30x is the top of that range.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: src/Makefile: nvcc -ccbin gcc-6, -O3 -Wno-deprecated-gpu-targets --use_fast_math -D_FORCE_INLINES -DCUDA_HOST_MALLOC; links cuFFT and cuBLAS. CUDA and gcc versions beyond gcc-6 not stated.
corrections.baseline: gpuNUFFT (GPU NUFFT gridding library), Fessler's Image Reconstruction Toolbox (IRT, MATLAB) and BART (the reproduction steps also build BART)
corrections.caveats: Tier B rests on the Magnetic Resonance in Medicine paper (2019), which could not be opened here (onlinelibrary.wiley.com is blocked); its abstract, seen through WebSearch, gives 6-30x depending on data set, so the README's 30x is the best case. GPU model and CUDA version are not on any page opened, so not tier A. The speedups are for radial-trajectory gridding against gpuNUFFT, BART and IRT, not against FFTW/MKL/KissFFT, and the repository description ('radial Fast Fourier Transform') overstates it as an FFT. The 75x is against CPU MATLAB code. Latest commits (Jan 2026) only zip MATLAB files; the CUDA code dates from 2018-2021. Reproduction needs MATLAB and git-lfs data.

notes: README numbers verified verbatim; Makefile and run script opened. Paper unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED); range 6-30x taken from a WebSearch summary of the abstract. Metadata matches: MIT (LICENSE opened), 32 stars, 10 forks, 19 commits, last 2026-01-12. Category 'fft' is a stretch (NUFFT gridding), but NUFFT fits the FFT family.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The benchmark code that runs dense cuFFT, SpFFT and the sparse variants is public (src/main.cu driver, src/dense_baseline.cu, src/sparse_fft_bluestein.cu, scripts/download_matrices.sh); the compiler (nvcc, CUDA 12.5.82), flags (CMakeLists.txt: Release, C++17, --expt-relaxed-constexpr -lineinfo, CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native) and the GPU (RTX 4090, driver 555.42.02) are stated. This matches the wave's precedent for GPU kernels that name the GPU (vsj001 SpMV, blackwell-tensorcore-kernels).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA Toolkit 12.5.82, CMake 3.20+, C++17; -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native; CMakeLists.txt adds CUDA options --expt-relaxed-constexpr -lineinfo
corrections.caveats: Course project (CSC 766) with no licence file (LICENSE 404, none shown on GitHub), so the code must not be copied. Wins only on mid-size non-power-of-2 sparse binary inputs: on sstmodel dense cuFFT takes 0.85 ms vs 1.39 ms and 3.62 ms for the sparse variants, and on the power-of-2 delaunay_n14 dense cuFFT takes 7.81 ms vs 68.56 ms and 304.76 ms. The fully custom variant is less accurate than dense cuFFT against the FFTW3 CPU reference (max_abs 2.0e-01 vs 4.7e-02 on benzene). The SpFFT figure is a single run. The dense baseline times only cufftExecR2C (plan creation and densification excluded). Host CPU not stated; the result is a GPU-kernel timing on one RTX 4090. The baseline is a dense GPU FFT that the workload is deliberately unfavourable to; not a general FFT speedup.

notes: All README numbers verified (benzene 23.64 / 14.65 / 9.60 ms, ~32 ms SpFFT, pct20stif 2,569 and 893 ms, losses on sstmodel and delaunay_n14). Upgraded to A on the reproducibility rule, but the code is unlicensed (reference only). Shortcomings worth recording: losses on small and power-of-2 inputs, lower accuracy of the custom variant.
